interest: This file provides valuable insight into the U.S. Navy's pre-World War II Japanese language training program, which produced critical intelligence officers and linguists who played pivotal roles in the Pacific War, notably Forrest R. Biard (who served at Station HYPO and at the Battle of Midway) and Gilven M. Slonim (who became a key intelligence officer on Admiral Chester Nimitz's staff). The 1939 correspondence documents the inter-departmental administrative protocol between the State and Navy Departments and highlights how Japan's 1934 policy decision to deny diplomatic accreditation to foreign military language officers was navigated on the eve of World War II. In addition, the included 1933 Far Eastern Affairs memorandum documents early Japanese naval posturing in Taiwan, quoting admirals who publicly identified Taiwan as a crucial front line of defense in light of mounting tensions with the United States.
overview: This State Department file (decimal file 894.32711) documents the assignment of United States Navy officers to Tokyo for Japanese language instruction, as well as earlier diplomatic monitoring of Japanese naval activities. The core of the file, dating from July and August 1939, comprises official correspondence between Acting Secretary of the Navy Charles Edison, Assistant Secretary of State Francis B. Sayre, and American Chargé d'Affaires ad interim in Tokyo Eugene H. Dooman concerning orders for Lieutenant (jg) Forrest R. Biard and Lieutenant (jg) Gilven M. Slonim to study Japanese in Tokyo under the administrative supervision of the Naval Attaché. The dispatches explicitly address the diplomatic and legal status of these officers, referencing Japan's late-1934 termination of diplomatic privileges for foreign service attachés' language students. Also filed within the bundle is an August 1933 Far Eastern Affairs memorandum summarizing a consular report from Taihoku on a Japanese fleet visit to Taiwan, noting bellicose statements by Japanese admirals regarding strained Japanese-American relations.

subfiles.about: The Navy Department informs the Secretary of State that Lieutenant (jg) Forrest R. Biard has been ordered to Tokyo to study the Japanese language.
subfiles.from: Charles Edison, Acting Secretary of the Navy
subfiles.summary: Acting Secretary of the Navy Charles Edison informs the Secretary of State of the Navy's intent to order Lieutenant (jg) Forrest R. Biard to Tokyo to study the Japanese language. Biard will report to the Naval Attaché at the American Embassy for administrative purposes only and will not be a member of the diplomatic staff. Biographical details are provided, including his June 1934 graduation from the U.S. Naval Academy and expected reporting date around October 1, 1939.
subfiles.title: Letter from Acting Secretary of the Navy Charles Edison regarding Japanese language study assignment of Lieutenant (jg) Forrest R. Biard

subfiles.about: The Department of State acknowledges the Navy Department's notification regarding Lieutenant (jg) Forrest R. Biard's assignment to Tokyo.
subfiles.from: Francis B. Sayre, Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.summary: Assistant Secretary of State Francis B. Sayre responds to Acting Secretary of the Navy Charles Edison's letter of July 19, 1939. He acknowledges the Navy Department's orders assigning Lieutenant (jg) Forrest R. Biard to Tokyo for Japanese language instruction under the administrative supervision of the Naval Attaché. Sayre confirms that appropriate instructions have been sent to the American Embassy in Tokyo.

subfiles.from: Francis B. Sayre, Assistant Secretary of State (for the Secretary of State)
subfiles.summary: Instruction No. 1781 informs American Chargé d'Affaires ad interim Eugene H. Dooman in Tokyo of the upcoming arrival of Lieutenant (jg) Forrest R. Biard for Japanese language study. The instruction notes that Biard will report to the Naval Attaché for administrative purposes only and will not hold official embassy staff status. It references Dooman's telegram of December 13, 1934 regarding Japan's decision to discontinue granting diplomatic status to foreign military and naval officers assigned for study.

subfiles.from: Charles Edison, Acting Secretary of the Navy
subfiles.summary: Acting Secretary of the Navy Charles Edison requests that diplomatic officers be notified of the Navy's intent to order Lieutenant (jg) Gilven M. Slonim to Tokyo to learn Japanese. Slonim is to report to the Naval Attaché at the American Embassy for administrative purposes only and will not form part of the official embassy staff. Slonim graduated from the U.S. Naval Academy in June 1936, attained his rank in June 1939, and is scheduled to report on October 1, 1939.

Sayre confirms that appropriate instructions have been dispatched to the American Embassy in Tokyo.

The communication emphasizes that Slonim will report to the Naval Attaché for administrative purposes only and will not hold official embassy status, citing the Japanese government's 1934 policy discontinuing diplomatic recognition for foreign military language students. Slonim's background details and intended reporting date of October 1, 1939 are provided.

subfiles.about: A State Department memorandum summarizes a consular report from Taihoku on a Japanese fleet visit to Taiwan and bellicose remarks by Japanese admirals.
subfiles.summary: An internal State Department memorandum reviews a despatch dated July 14, 1933, from the American consulate in Taihoku reporting on visits to Taiwan by three Japanese royal princes accompanying the Japanese fleet. The memorandum highlights press remarks by two Japanese admirals emphasizing Taiwan's frontline role in national defense and noting that relations with the United States had become strained. It records that relevant sections of the despatch were forwarded to the Naval Attaché in Tokyo to be shared with the Navy Department.
subfiles.title: State Department Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Taihoku Despatch Regarding Fleet Visit to Taiwan
